units.translation: an interjection expressing various emotions, as in Latin a

(which in the oldest manuscripts is written with the single letter a): hence by the grammarians it is called ἐπίρρημα ἐκπληκτικόν, θαυμαστικόν, κελευστικόν, σχετλιαστικὸν [an adverb of astonishment, wonder, command, or lamentation]: about which I have said more in the Lexicon Sophocleum. There are six examples in Aeschylus, and not many in Sophocles and Euripides.
before dochmiacs ἆ ἆ [ah! ah!] rightly deleted in the copies
which in M is written ἀζηνιουσίω [azeniouio]
Doubled, it expresses wonder at something sudden
Outside the verse where Orestes thinks he sees the Furies approaching

Before a bacchiac verse, where Prometheus perceives the chorus of Oceanids approaching, I deleted ἔα ἔα [ah! ah!], which arose from the letters é written above, by which the gloss έα έα [ah! ah!] is indicated, as is clear from verse 566, where Io exclaims ἆ ἆ, χρίει τις αὖ με τὸν τάλαιναν οΐστρος [ah! ah! the gadfly stings me again, wretched me], where in M after ἆ ἆ [ah! ah!] only the letters ἒ ἔ [e e] were added, which I deleted, but in the copies ἆ ἆ ἔα ἔα [ah! ah! ah! ah!] was interpolated. Moreover, I have shown in the Lexicon Sophocleum that doubled ἆ [ah!] is more correctly written ἀᾶ [a-a], according to the analogy of other interjections, and indeed so that it has the measure not of a spondee but of an iamb, which is recommended by the example of Aeschylus Ag. 1125, where the iambic tripody àâ, idoù idoú [ah! ah! behold! behold!] in the strophe corresponds to a tripody beginning with a pure iamb ἐή παπαϊ παπαϊ [e! alas! alas!], just as in Euripides the iamb ὀλεῖς [you will destroy] placed in the antistrophe Or. v. 158 corresponds to ἀᾶ [a-a] in the strophe v. 146

The letters in M in a damaged place ό ό ό ά ά ά [o o o a a a] Hermannus referred to the interjection ἆ [ah!] with little probability, writing ὂ ὂ ἂ ἄ [o o a a], which certainly should be written ὀὼ ἀᾶ [o-o a-a]. More probably one may conjecture ὅρα ὅρα [look! look!], to which ὁρῶ [I see] agrees, which follows in v. 830
Apollo, Apollo! Ah, where have you brought me? To what house?
Ah, Zeus, Io's wrath, a pursuer from the gods,
Ah! ah! Behold, behold! Keep away from the cow.
Ah! ah! What women are these, like Gorgons—?
Ah! ah! ah! ah! What sound, what scent flies at me, unseen?

Bekker's Anecdota p. 321, 19 and Suidas ἀβδέλυκτα [not to be loathed]: ἀμύσακτα, ἀμίαντα, τὰ μὴ μιαίνοντα, ἃ οὐκ ἄν τις βδελυχθείη καὶ δυσχεράνειε [unpolluted, undefiled, things that do not defile, which no one would loathe or be disgusted at]. τραγικωτέρα δὲ ἡ λέξις [the word is rather tragic]. Similarly Zonaras Lex. p. 9 and the grammarian in Cramer's Anecdota Parisiensia vol. 4 p. 85, 23. Bekker corrected the reading of his manuscript and of Suidas γὰρ ἀβδέλυκτ᾽ ἐμοὶ [for not loathed by me]. άβδέλυκτά μοι [not loathed by me] Anecdota Parisiensia.
Indeed, I love these things, and they are not loathsome to me.
